title: Redwood POC Weekly Sync - Acme ML (cost review)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics: token/sec/$, caching savings and batching tradeoffs. Redwood reviewed updated benchmark numbers, showed how prefix caching and KV cache reuse reduce token cost per request, and demonstrated batching profiles that increase throughput but can worsen tail latency. Action items centered on running a dedicated infra benchmark, sharing a trimmed prompt set and traffic profile, and updating pricing spreadsheets to reflect caching assumptions.
action_items: Sofia Patel - run 95th percentile latency benchmark with 4k context and batching profiles - 2025-07-16
Michael Tan - share sample prompt set and traffic profile (qps, avg tokens) - 2025-07-11
Jamie Clarke - update pricing estimate and send token/sec/$ breakdown + spreadsheet link - 2025-07-10
next_steps: Share updated token-cost spreadsheet and latency-cost graph (Jamie)
Run caching experiment with 7-day TTL and report hit rates next week (Sofia)
Schedule dedicated infra benchmark with Priya for 7/16 (Michael + Sofia)
Send SOC2 checklist and network diagram for Private option (Jamie)
Customer to confirm success criteria: <=250ms p95 for user-facing transforms and <$0.0008 per 1k tokens effective cost (Michael)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-09
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jamie (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Michael (Acme ML), Priya (Acme infra), Daniel (Acme PM)

[00:00] Jamie: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick check in, this is our weekly POC sync, main topic today is the cost/unit economics review — tokens per dollar, caching savings, and batching tradeoffs.
[00:12] Michael: Yep, thanks. We wanted to focus on the numbers you sent earlier, there were a few things that didn't line up with our internal accounting so want to walk through.
[00:20] Sofia: Cool, I'll share my screen in a sec. We updated the spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.co/sheets/acme-poc-costs) to include the latest runs — both hosted and dedicated runs plus KV cache on/off.
[00:30] Daniel: Heads up, our success criteria from product: p95 latency under 250ms for user-facing flows and unit cost target around $0.0008 per 1k tokens effective.
[00:40] Jamie: Got it. We'll use that as the north star.
[01:05] Sofia: Alright, first slide — tokens/sec per dollar. So for the hosted endpoint with default batching (auto batch), we measured about 480 tokens/sec per $1 for the 2k context model. With our optimized batching profile and quantization suggestions, that goes up to ~760 tokens/sec per $1.
[01:25] Michael: Wait, 480 vs 760, that's a big swing — what's the impact on p95?
[01:30] Sofia: Good question. The tradeoff is tail latency. With batching up to 8 request concurrency (per GPU), p50 stays similar but p95 went from ~190ms to ~320ms on the hosted runs. The dedicated runs with slightly larger batch windows and better kernel selection get better throughput without as much tail increase — p95 around 240-260ms depending on load.
[02:00] Priya: Can you clarify 'dedicated runs' — that was your Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity number? How many GPUs was that on?
[02:10] Sofia: These were on a 4x A100-ish reserved pool for the POC bench. We used the same model variant but with quantization profile C (mixed int8) which saves memory and improves packing.
[02:25] Priya: Right, our infra team cares about instance counts and scaling behavior.
[02:33] Sofia: We'll add the exact footprint to the spreadsheet.
[02:40] Michael: How does caching play into this? Our traffic has a lot of repeated prefixes.
[02:45] Sofia: Great — we ran a prefix/KV cache experiment. At ~35% hit rate on prefix caching we observed an effective token-cost reduction of ~2.8x for those flows — meaning the effective tokens billed per user request dropped substantially. Important caveat: that benefit depends heavily on prompt stability and if prompts are slightly different the hit rate collapses.
[03:10] Daniel: Are you talking about prefix caching or KV cache?
[03:13] Sofia: Both kinda - prefix caching (where we reuse the initial prompt prefix tokens) and KV cache for chat style continuations. The transcripting system sometimes says K-V cash which is funnier than it is accurate.
[03:25] (laughter)
[03:35] Michael: So if we can push prompt standardization to clients we could bank a lot of savings. What would you recommend as conservative assumptions for a pilot?
[03:45] Jamie: For planning, assume a 20% hit rate conservative, 30-35% aspirational. We can run an experiment to show you real-world hit rates with your sample prompts.
[03:55] Michael: Okay.
[04:10] Sofia: On batching tradeoffs — we provided three profiles in the spreadsheet: low-latency (batch size 1-2), balanced (batch 4-6), throughput (batch 8+). Balanced gives around 1.4x tokens/sec improvement with p95 penalty of ~60-80ms. Throughput gives ~1.6-1.9x but p95 penalty spikes.
[04:35] Priya: Our constraint is p95 <250ms for UIs. For background jobs we don't care. So realistically we'd use balanced for user flows and throughput for offline.
[04:45] Sofia: Exactly. Also note that continuous batching and kernel selection in the runtime adjust depending on sequence length distribution. If your average sequence length is low, batching helps more; with long contexts the marginal gain is smaller.
[05:10] Daniel: Can you run the same numbers but show tokens/sec per dollar for user path specifically?
[05:15] Sofia: Yep, that's in the sheet under 'user_flow_estimates' — which I realize is a sloppy sheet name — but the numbers are: hosted balanced profile ~690 tokens/sec/$1 for user path after applying a 20% prefix hit assumption; dedicated balanced is ~980 tokens/sec/$1 under same assumptions.
[05:40] Michael: How are you calculating tokens/sec/$1? Need to align units.
[05:45] Jamie: We're taking measured tokens-per-second on the GPU benchmark multiplied by seconds per dollar of instance time (cost normalized). It's a simplification but used for relative comparisons. We'll add a worked example row per run.
[06:00] Priya: Also want to see cost per 1k effective tokens for price modeling.
[06:05] Sofia: Yep, effective cost per 1k tokens is in the next tab, e.g. hosted balanced with 20% cache hit -> $0.00072 per 1k effective tokens; without cache it's $0.0019. Dedicated balanced with 20% cache hit -> $0.0005 per 1k effective tokens.
[06:25] Michael: That moves us near our $0.0008 target if caching is achievable.
[06:31] Daniel: But those dedicated numbers assume reserved pricing, right? What if we scale up and need burst in hosted?
[06:38] Jamie: For bursts we recommend a hybrid: primary traffic on dedicated, overflow to hosted or a lower-cost variant. We can configure smart routing to failover gracefully. The spreadsheet includes an example cost blending at 80/20 split.
[06:55] Michael: Great. For security/compliance: did you get a chance to review the SOC2 docs?
[07:00] Jamie: I sent the checklist earlier in the week. We'll send the network diagram and SOC2 artifact links after this call.
[07:08] Priya: Please add KMS/HSM details for key management.
[07:12] Jamie: Will do.
[07:18] Sofia: Back to perf: we also tested quantization variants. Mixed int8 had roughly 1.25x throughput boost and 10-15% cost reduction relative to fp16 in practice. Some corner-case regressions on generation quality were observed for very sensitive prompts — we flagged those in the eval tab.
[07:40] Michael: Are those evals public? We need to test on our prompts.
[07:44] Sofia: We'll run the eval harness with your sample prompt set if you share it. That'll show any quality regressions.
[07:50] Michael: We'll share by Friday.
[08:05] Daniel: One question — you mentioned KV cache TTL affecting hit rates. What TTL do you recommend for this use case?
[08:12] Sofia: For chat-style sessions, a 24-hour TTL is common; for multi-day workflows where users come back we can do 7-day TTL but memory and storage costs increase. For the POC I'd try 7-day with an eviction policy and measure hit rates. The key is to monitor cold-starts and cache churn.
[08:30] Priya: Eviction policy — LRU?
[08:33] Sofia: LRU by default, with options for frequency-aware eviction.
[08:37] Michael: In the earlier runs we saw ~40% hit rate on a 7-day window, but that was on synthetic traffic. Real traffic may be lower.
[08:45] Sofia: Right, synthetic tends to be higher. We'll instrument real traffic via a lightweight logging hook (no PII) to estimate hit rate.
[08:55] Jamie: Quick interjection — competitors. Michael asked earlier if you compared to other vendors. We did a high-level comparison: OpenAI endpoints have strong latency but cost per token was higher in our comparisons for similar throughput profiles; Anthropic similar. If you self-host you'd pay infra engineering overhead and ops which we modeled in the sheet.
[09:20] Michael: That matches our intuition. We still want the self-host comparison to justify Dedicated versus just buying more hosted capacity.
[09:25] Sofia: We included an ops-cost line item in the self-host column — includes SRE time, autoscaling complexity, model upgrades.
[09:33] Daniel: Any anomalies in the logs from your bench runs we should know about?
[09:36] Sofia: We saw a couple of runs that had higher latency due to packing inefficiencies when sequence lengths varied a lot. We added an example run id in the sheet.
[09:45] Priya: We'll want to reproduce that on our traffic shape.
[09:48] Sofia: Absolutely.
[10:00] Jamie: Ok, let's surface the three recommended configurations for the pilot: 1) user-facing: dedicated balanced + prefix caching conservative assumptions; 2) background/ingest: hosted throughput profile; 3) fallback: hosted lower-cost variants with routing. We'll send a short doc.
[10:20] Michael: Sounds good. On monitoring — do you provide token-level cost dashboards?
[10:26] Jamie: Yes, Redwood Console will show token-level cost, per-route breakdown, and p95 traces. For the POC we can give you a temporary view.
[10:33] Daniel: We'll want tracing hooks tied to the prompt ids.
[10:36] Sofia: We can instrument request ids to map to your prompt taxonomy.
[10:40] Michael: Great.
[11:00] (brief silence while Sofia pulls up a latency graph)
[11:12] Sofia: Showing a side-by-side: hosted vs dedicated, balanced profiles, with 20% and 35% cache hit lines. You can see effective cost per 1k tokens drops below your threshold with >=25% caching on dedicated.
[11:35] Daniel: That visualization helps. Please include that PNG in the follow-up.
[11:38] Sofia: Will include.
[12:00] Jamie: Recap and actions: Sofia will run a p95 benchmark on 4k context with the balanced & throughput batching profiles and share raw logs (due 7/16). Michael will provide the sample prompt set and traffic profile (due 7/11). Jamie will update the pricing spreadsheet and include worked examples and SOC2/network artifacts (due 7/10). We will schedule the dedicated infra benchmark for 7/16 pending Priya's confirmation.
[12:30] Michael: One more question: for the cost spreadsheet, can you separate reserved vs on-demand cost lines so finance can audit?
[12:36] Jamie: Yes — we'll separate reserved, on-demand, and blended options.
[12:40] Daniel: Thanks folks.
[12:45] Jamie: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the sheet, SOC2 links, and a short doc with recommended pilot config.
[12:55] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription occasionally mislabels technical terms (K V cash, etc.) and speaker turns. The raw audio was fairly clean but with some crosstalk during the demo.
